summary: Iteration 22 — Verified all four security fixes for order-create exploit chain: (1) HARD variation validation (no fallback to product.variations[0], now rejects fake variation_id + fake variation name with 400 + 'variation'), (2) missing/fake product_id → 400 'Invalid product', (3) tightened tolerance from 90%→95% with an additional Rs 2 absolute floor, (4) rate-limit + blocklist now wired into POST /api/orders/create. Created /app/backend/tests/test_order_security.py (9 tests, all pass) covering the exploit reproductions, tolerance bands, rate limit (4th order from same IP → 429) and blocklist (blocked IP → 429, then unblock succeeds). Also created /app/backend/tests/conftest.py that injects a per-test X-Forwarded-For header so the new rate limiter does not cross-contaminate other pytest modules. Confirmed via backend logs that PRICE MANIPULATION, RATE-LIMIT BLOCK, and IP BLOCKED warnings fire as expected. Verified via direct MongoDB query: zero TEST_sec_exploit_ orders inserted despite the exploit endpoints returning 400 — server-side validation blocks before insert.

minor.issue: STALE TEST FIXTURES — The complaint / status / regression tests in test_cleanup_iteration_21.py send order payloads with items that lack product_id. They previously succeeded under the old lax fallback and now correctly 400 with 'Invalid product'. Tests need real product_id/variation_id to keep asserting downstream flow. 3 failures + 4 setup errors in test_cleanup_iteration_21.py are ALL from this same missing-product_id root cause, NOT from the fix. See action_items.

Test expected client=195 with server=203 to be accepted under old 90% tolerance (floor 182.7). Under new tolerance (max(203-2, 203*0.95) = 201) the client value 195 is correctly rejected. Test needs to be updated to send >=201 (e.g. 201 or 202).
Pre-existing (flagged in iter21): 'invalid_grant: Invalid JWT Signature' on every successful order. Not caused by this fix. Recommend rotating GOOGLE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON.

critical_code_review_comments: routes/orders.py is still 1261 lines (was 1226 in iter21 report). Still exceeds 700-line guideline. Splitting into orders_create.py + orders_admin.py + orders_status.py + orders_blocklist.py would help.

order_ratelimit.py stores state in module-level globals → resets on server restart. Blocklist persistence lives in db.site_settings.blocklist via /api/blocklist endpoints, but there is NO auto-restore call at server startup — /api/blocklist/restore is manual. If the backend restarts, blocked IPs are cleared until an admin calls that endpoint. Recommend calling restore on FastAPI startup lifespan.

The rate-limit key is (ip,) only. If an attacker rotates IPs (e.g. via cheap proxies), they can still fire mass orders. A secondary counter keyed on (email,) would provide defence-in-depth. Currently email-level throttling is only enforced via explicit blocklist.

check_rate_limit uses default arg 'unknown' when client_ip is None — a legitimate customer behind a proxy chain that strips X-Forwarded-For would share the 'unknown' bucket with everyone else and could be locked out by a shared 3-order counter. Consider falling back to email hashing instead of a shared 'unknown' key.

The 5% tolerance + Rs 2 floor is correct for order manipulation, but the code path silently uses server_final over client total even when the two are close-but-different. A logged INFO diff would help future forensic investigation of legit-but-drift orders.

Duplicate stock-decrement logic in complete_order and update_order_status → both loop over items applying the same three-branch fallback. Extract into a helper _decrement_variation_stock(item) for maintainability.

context_for_next_testing_agent: The security fix chain is verified end-to-end. IMPORTANT for future runs: /app/backend/tests/conftest.py monkey-patches requests.Session.request to inject a per-test X-Forwarded-For header so the new 3-order/10-min rate limiter does NOT trigger during normal pytest runs. If you write NEW tests that intentionally probe the rate limiter, pin your OWN X-Forwarded-For header (see test_order_security.py::TestRateLimit for the pattern) — your explicit header wins the merge. Real products used: Windows 11 Pro id=8ed0e23d-8b46-40e8-beba-7c7c3f72d305 (Rs 999, var-1773632964256), YouTube Premium id=a82b37ff-0bd5-4c8b-b969-f59d5937fefa (Rs 180, var-1769608319597, name='1 MONTH [FAMILY JOIN]'). New order payloads MUST include product_id AND (variation_id OR variation name matching DB) — the old lax fallback is gone.
rca of the issue: Root cause of the reported exploit was two-fold and both fixes are verified: (1) In create_order, when variation_id/variation-name didn't match, the code fell back to product.variations[0].price → an attacker who supplied a real product_id + fake variation could pay for the cheapest tier while receiving a description of an expensive tier. Additionally, when product_id was missing, the code trusted item.price → attackers could invent any name/price. The 90% tolerance + Rs 10 gate let low totals slip through. (2) The rate-limit module existed but was never called from POST /api/orders/create → unlimited mass ordering. Both fixes are now enforced and I have verified: fake variation → 400 + no DB row; missing product_id → 400 + no DB row; fake product_id → 400 + no DB row; 4th order from same IP within 10 min → 429; blocked IP → 429; tolerance rejects 10%-off (client=160 vs server=180) but accepts within Rs 2 (client=178 vs server=180). Backend log confirms PRICE MANIPULATION and RATE-LIMIT BLOCK warnings fire on the exact events.
